text:
IN THE SUPREME
COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Pitt v. Holt,

2007 BCSC 1555

Date: 20071023

Docket:
E062119

Registry: Vancouver

Between:

Aaron Sean Pitt

Plaintiff

And

Sherri Louise Holt

and William Arthur Holt

Defendants

Before:
The Honourable Mr. Justice Cohen

Reasons for Judgment

Counsel for the plaintiff

B.L.
Scheirer

Counsel for the defendant, Sherri Louise Holt

J.
Lewis

Counsel for the defendant, William Holt

F.
Lamer

Date and Place
of Hearing:

September 11, 2007

Vancouver,
B.C.

I.          The Application

[
1
]

This is an application by the defendants for
dismissal of the plaintiff’s action pursuant to Rules 18 and 19(24) of the
Rules
of Court
,
B.C. Reg. 221/90
, on the grounds that the action is entirely
without merit and an abuse of process, and in the alternative for security for
costs based on the same grounds.

II.         Background

[
2
]

The plaintiff Aaron Sean Pitt (“Pitt”) and the
defendant Sherri Louise Holt (“Holt”) began cohabitating in October 1998.  They
were married on July 31, 1999.  Holt had two children from a previous
relationship (Zevan and Shirai Feen).  A third child (Trinity) was born of the
relationship between the parties on December 18, 1999.

[
3
]

Following Trinity’s birth, the parties decided
to purchase a property at
253 East 27
th
Street, in North Vancouver
(the “property”) as their matrimonial home.  Pitt’s grandparents provided
$25,000 as a down payment.  The defendant William Arthur Holt (“William”),
Holt’s father, acted as a co-signer under the mortgage loan and went on title
with the parties as a one-third owner of the property in joint tenancy.

[
4
]

The parties separated in April 2004.  They
entered into a separation agreement dated June 24, 2004 (the “separation
agreement”).  The separation agreement provides,
inter alia
, that the
sum of $27,629 was to be paid to Pitt in consideration for a transfer by him to
Holt of all of his “interest, right and title to and in” the property.  The
parties made no provision for maintenance.

III.        The Legal Proceedings

[
5
]

On February 2, 2005, Holt commenced proceedings
in Provincial Court to compel payment of child maintenance.  In her reasons for
judgment Baird Ellan P.C.J. held that Pitt had acted in
loco parentis
in
relation to the children Zevan and Shirai Feen and that they were therefore
considered to be his children for child support purposes.  Pitt was found
liable to pay child maintenance of $300 for these children, retroactive to
February 1, 2005, and required to pay one-third of the extraordinary expenses
for these children.  No child maintenance was ordered for the child Trinity,
but Pitt was ordered to pay one-half of the extraordinary expenses for this
child (due to a joint custody order for this child).

[
6
]

Pitt commenced this action on June 16, 2006.  He
seeks an order for equal division of family assets.  He alleges that William
has no beneficial or other interest in the property and that he holds title to
a one-half interest in the property in trust for and on behalf of the parties.  He
also alleges,
inter alia
, that Holt and William colluded to deprive him
of his rightful interest in the property and that Holt made material
misrepresentations to him respecting the interest of William in the property
with the intention and effect of depriving him of his interest and fair
entitlement to his share of the property.  Pitt seeks relief under the
Family
Relations Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 128 (the “
Act
”),
inter
alia
, pursuant to
s. 66
, a determination of ownership, right of possession
and division of property, including the vesting of property under
s. 65
as may
be appropriate under the circumstances; pursuant to
s. 66
, an order fixing the
monetary sum to be paid by Holt and William to Pitt as compensation for the
purpose of adjusting the division of property.

[
7
]

On January 23, 2007, Pitt testified in
Provincial Court that he could not pay the extraordinary expenses and child
support he had been ordered to pay because he had not been working since
December 2006.  He also testified that he could not pay extraordinary expenses
for Trinity and that he was borrowing money to live.  Baird Ellan P.C.J. stayed
the retroactive child support and payment of the retroactive extraordinary
expenses and arrears for one month.

IV.       The Issues

(1)       Should
the “in trust” claim against William be dismissed?

(2)       Should
Pitt’s claim for misrepresentation be dismissed?

(3)       Should Pitt’s claim for an order setting aside the
separation agreement be dismissed?

(4)       Is Pitt’s action an abuse of process?

(5)       Should
Pitt be ordered to post security for costs?

V.        The
Legal Test

[
8
]

The defence brings this application pursuant to
Rules 18(6) and 19(24) (b) and (d).

[
9
]

Rule 18(6) provides:

In an action in which an appearance has been
entered, the defendant may, on the ground there is no merit in the whole or
part of the claim, apply to the court for judgment on an affidavit setting out
the facts verifying the defendant's contention that there is no merit in the
whole or part of the claim and stating that the deponent knows of no facts
which would substantiate the whole or part of the claim.

[
10
]

On an application under Rule 18(6), the court
may make an order for summary judgment in favour of a defendant dismissing an
action only where a plaintiff is “bound to lose”.  Another way of stating the
test is whether there is a bona fide triable issue to be determined:
Serup
v. Board of Trustees of School District #57
,
1989 CanLII 5192 (BC CA)
, 57 D.L.R. (4th) 261 at
264, 54 B.C.L.R. (2d) 258 (C.A.).  In
Skybridge Investments Ltd. v. Metro
Motors Ltd.

(c.o.b. Metro Ford)
,
2006 BCCA 500
, 61
B.C.L.R. (4th) 241, Thackray J.A. at paras. 10 – 13 states, as follows:

A judge hearing an application pursuant to Rule
18(6) must: examine the pleaded facts to determine which causes of action they
may support; identify the essential elements required to be proved at trial in
order to succeed on each cause of action; and determine if sufficient material
facts have been pleaded to support each element of a given cause of action.

If
insufficient
material facts have been
pleaded to support every element of a cause of action, then beyond a doubt that
cause of action is bound to fail and a defendant bringing an application
pursuant to Rule 18(6) will have met the onus to negative the existence of a
bona
fide
triable issue.

If
sufficient
material facts have been
pleaded to support every element of a cause of action, but one or more of those
pleaded material facts are contested, then the judge ruling on a Rule 18(6)
application is not to weigh the evidence to determine the issue of fact for the
purpose of the application.  The judge’s function is limited to a determination
as to whether a
bona fide
triable issue arises on the material before
the court in the context of the applicable law.  If a judge ruling on a Rule
18(6) application must assess and weigh the evidence to arrive at a summary
judgment, the “plain and obvious” or “beyond a doubt” test has not been met.

On appeal, as on the application in chambers,
the question addressed in a Rule 18(6) application of whether there is a
bona
fide
issue to be tried must be decided assuming that the uncontested
material facts as pleaded by the plaintiff are true:
Van Den Akker v. Naudi,

[1997] B.C.J. No. 1649, 1997 CarswellBC 1470 (B.C.C.A.)
.

[
11
]

In the instant case, Pitt argues that the test
provides a low hurdle and that there is no question but that there are bona
fide triable issues.

[
12
]

Rule 19(24)(b) and (d) provides:

(24)     At any stage of a proceeding the court
may order to be struck out or amended the whole or any part of an endorsement,
pleading, petition or other document on the ground that

(b)       it is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous
or vexatious,

…

(d)       it is otherwise an abuse of the
process of the court,

and the court may grant judgment or order the
proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and may order the costs of the application
to be paid as special costs.

[
13
]

A scandalous allegation will not be struck if it
is relevant to the proceedings.  A pleading is “unnecessary” or “vexatious” if
it does not go to establishing the plaintiff’s cause of action or does not
advance a claim known in law.  A pleading is “frivolous” if it is unsustainable
because of the doctrine of estoppel: see
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform
Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress
,
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, 36 C.P.C. (4th) 266, [1999] B.C.J.
No. 2160 (QL)(S.C.) at para.
47
.

[
14
]

The applicability of the doctrine of
res
judicata
must be plain and obvious before a statement of claim will be
struck out: see
Lehndorff Management Ltd. v. L.R.S. Development
Enterprises Ltd.
(1980),
1980 CanLII 393 (BC CA)
, 19 B.C.L.R. 59 at 66, 109 D.L.R. (3d) 729
(C.A.).

[
15
]

In
Chapman v. Canada
,
2003 BCCA
665
, 21 B.C.L.R. (4th) 272, Saunders J.A. at paras. 12 – 14 states, as follows:

The criteria for application of all provisions
of Rule 19(24) are established in authorities considered by the chambers judge:

Hunt v. T & N plc,

1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959 (S.C.C.);
Berscheid v.
Ensign,
1999 CanLII 6494 (BC SC)
, [1999] B.C.J. No. 1172 (B.C.S.C.);
Babavic v. Babowech,

[1993] B.C.J. No. 1802 (B.C.S.C.)
,
World Wide Treasure Adventures Inc. v.
Trivia Games Inc.
(1996),
1996 CanLII 1428 (BC CA)
, 17 B.C.L.R. (3d) 187 (B.C.C.A.), and
Kripps v.
Touche Ross & Co.
(1990),
1990 CanLII 937 (BC CA)
, 48 B.C.L.R. (2d) 171 (B.C.C.A.).  The test is
whether it is plain and obvious that the impugned pleading has the fault
alleged.  Otherwise the party whose pleading is challenged is entitled to a
trial of the issue.

The orders in this case were made under Rule
19(24)(a) and (d).  Thus in order to succeed the applicant is required to
establish that it is plain and obvious that the pleadings disclose no cause of
action (Rule 19(24)(a)) or that the proceedings are an abuse of process (Rule
19(24)(d)).  Otherwise the litigation will be allowed to proceed.

On an application under Rule 19(24)(a) for an
order that the pleading discloses no reasonable claim, no evidence is permitted
to be adduced (Rule 19(27)), and the matter must proceed on the pleading
alone.  Rule 19(24)(d), concerning abuse of process, on the other hand, may be
considered with reference to evidence.  As the concepts of
res judicata

and collateral attack on a court order are both encompassed by the concept of
abuse of process, evidence is permitted to be adduced on a Rule 19(24)(d)
application as to the circumstances that are said to characterize the claim as
abusive.

Pitt argues that there is nothing about his
pleadings that would support an order for the striking of them or any part of
them in this case.  He asserts that his is an ordinary family law case seeking
divorce and a division of family assets in circumstances in which there is an
unfair separation agreement.

VI.       The “In Trust” Claim

[
16
]

Clause 14(b) of the separation agreement reads,
as follows:

14(b)   Forthwith upon execution of this
agreement, the Wife shall purchase from the Husband, all interest, right, and
title to and in the matrimonial home upon the following terms and conditions:
[…]

[
17
]

Pitt’s position is that the property was
purchased by him and Holt and that William was not entitled to any of the
equity, having made no contributions to the property.  He also asserts that the
separation agreement was settled between the parties on the basis of factual
and legal inaccuracies.  He claims that it provided for the division of only
one of the family assets, the property, on the basis of its assessed value for
2003 and on the basis that William has a one-third beneficial interest in the
property.  He says that no one knew what the property was actually worth as
there was no appraisal.  Therefore, he submits, the separation agreement is
null and void and a proper division of family assets ought to be made at trial.

[
18
]

The main thrust of Pitt’s claim is that the
separation agreement was signed by him without legal advice and that it is
unfair.  He contends that William went on the title of the property as a one-third
owner only because he was required to do so by the bank as a co-signer.  He
insists that it was not the case that the parties would not have been able to
purchase the property if it was not for William.

[
19
]

To establish that William holds his one-third
interest in trust, Pitt refers to evidence from the examination for discovery
of William.  He testified that he did not contribute financially in any way to
the property and when he was asked if he ever had any discussions with either
Pitt or Holt about the nature of certain renovations they made to the property
he replied, “No. It wasn’t my business.”  He also testified, “My wife. We
discussed it, and I said to Marilyn, ‘you understand that we’re putting
ourselves on the line for this house for those kids?’  At the time we thought
everything was going to be rosy, you know, that things were going to progress.  Aaron
would—you know, they’d go forward and there wouldn’t be a problem.  And
possibly somewhere down the road they would take on the new mortgage, the two
of them, and I would get out with a little bit of compensation for tying myself
up for those years, and that would be the end of it.  As it happened, nothing
like that happened.”

[
20
]

Pitt also refers to the examination for
discovery testimony of Holt where she testified when asked whether she had any
discussions with the bank, “No. They drew up the contract, and that’s how it
was signed.  I’m not a bank specialist or a contract specialist.  We were just
buying our first home together.”  She was then asked, “’We’ being you and Mr.
Pitt?” and she answered, “With my father’s credit.”

[
21
]

However, at his examination for discovery, Pitt
admitted that he knew and understood that in the separation agreement he parted
with any and all of his interest in the property:

Q         All
right.  And then at paragraph 14(b), 14 (a) was crossed off, and you can see
your initials there.  I'm sorry, AP.  And then immediately at 14(b), there is
the essence of the deal which is: "The payment to the husband/wife of the
sum of $27,629."  And then below that: “The above amount will be paid out
as of August 31st, 2004, in full.  Until such time, Aaron Sean Pitt will
continue to pay mortgage for two months prior to the payout for a total of
$1,655."

A         M'mm-hmm.

Q         Did
you read that?

A         M'mm-hmm.

Q         You
understood that?

A         Yes.

Q         There's
nothing complicated with that?

A         I
understood it.

Q         So
your evidence is you let go of your half of the matrimonial home; right?

A         Yes.

Q         For
$27,629?

A         Yes.

Q         Plus
two mortgage payments?

A         Yes.

[
22
]

Pitt also admitted that, two months later, he
signed a form of transfer of his interest in the property to Holt and William.

[
23
]

In effect, Pitt asserts that the arrangement
between the parties is different from what was provided for in the purchase
agreement.  The purchase agreement provides that the parties and William will
each be a one-third owner as joint tenants: the amendments necessary in order
to add William as a purchaser were in fact initialled by Pitt.  On this point,
Pitt’s discovery testimony is that he did not understand the purchase agreement
to represent such an outcome:

Q         But
what's fairly clear, though, is that you agreed that Mr. Pitt would have to be
a third owner of the property?

A         Mr.
Pitt?

Q         I'm
sorry.  Mr. Holt.

A         To
be honest, I didn't realize the significance of being on title.  In my mind he
was just a co-signer of the mortgage.

Q         I
see.

A         And
I never in the relationship, the years I lived in the house, ever considered
him to be an owner of the house in any way, shape or form.  He was a guarantor of
the mortgage.

Q         So
you didn't think he was going to purchase a one-third interest in the home.  Is
that what you're saying?

A         No.

Q         I'm
going to show you a contract of purchase and sale then dated, as best as I can
make out, June 23rd, 2002.  Do you see that?

A         Yeah.

Q         That's
a contract of purchase and sale whereby you acquired an interest in the home?

A         Right.

MR.
LAMER:  Let's mark that as Exhibit number 2.

EXHIBIT 2:  Contract
of purchase and sale dated June 23, 2002

MR.
LAMER:

Q         Just
so I get it straight, you didn't really think that Mr. Holt would be an owner
of the property?

A         No.

Q         But
if I look at this agreement of purchase and sale, it's in typed terms here.  It
says "Aaron Pitt"; right?

A         Yes.

Q         And
then there's a handwritten amendment with some initials on it?

A         Right.

Q         Do
you see that?

A         Yes.

Q         I
take it one of these initials is yours?

A         Yeah.

Q         All
right.

A         Yes.

Q         So
there was a change in the contract:  add Sherri Holt and William Holt as
buyers?

A         Right.

Q         What
is it about that that you didn't understand?

A         I
knew that it was necessary for him to be on title for some reason, but I didn't
consider him a buyer of the property.  I just knew that he was helping us out to
buy a home by having his name on there because we had such a weak portfolio
that we couldn't get one on our own.

Q         But
what you're saying, though, is -- I just want to get your evidence correctly.
You're saying that adding Sherri Holt and William Holt beside the caption
"buyer" didn't make them buyers of the property?

A         I
didn't see it that way.  All I know is we faxed him some mortgage documents,
and he signed the mortgage documents so we could get our home.

[
24
]

However, the purchase agreement makes it plain
that the parties and William were purchasing the property as joint owners.

[
25
]

In my opinion, Pitt cannot now claim through
oral testimony that the purchase agreement was other than it states.  Even
assuming an ambiguity in an agreement, which I find there is not, the law is
settled that a party cannot contradict through oral evidence the terms of a
written document: see
Sultani v. Blenz the Canadian Coffee Co.
,

2005 BCCA 578
, 218 B.C.A.C. 288.  Moreover, evidence of a party’s subjective
understanding of an agreement is irrelevant and inadmissible in aid of the
interpretation of contractual provisions: see
Carter v. Sigmund
(1996),

1996 CanLII 2138 (BC CA)
, 75 B.C.A.C. 93, 123 W.A.C. 93 (B.C.C.A.), at paras.
11 and 14
;
MacDonald
v. Grant
(1993),
1993 CanLII 1164 (BC SC)
, 85 B.C.L.R. (2d) 180, 35 R.P.R. (2d) 50 (S.C.), at
paras.
47 and 53
;
Toronto Dominion Bank v. Leigh Instruments Ltd.
,

1998 CanLII 14806 (ON CTGD)
, 1998 CarswellOnt. 2565 (WLeC), 40 B.L.R. (2d) 1 (Ont. C.J.), at para.
410
.

[
26
]

In any event, Pitt admitted that the purchase
agreement contemplated that William was purchasing a one-third interest in the
property and that this “was the deal”:

Q         So,
for example, when you were asked to approve the addition of Sherri Holt and
William Holt, you didn't pay attention to that?

A         No.

Q         So
you signed blindly?

A         No.
There was an understanding.  We -- they had accepted our down payment.  We had
accepted the purchase price.  Things are in place.  We needed a co-signer in
order to get the mortgage.  I was signing where I needed to sign so that we
could get to where we needed to go.

Q         All
right.  There was no dispute about any of this?  It was just --

A         No.

Q         No.  It was a pleasant, positive
atmosphere, wasn't it.  Right?

A         Yes.

Q         I'm
going to show you another document.  It is a contract of purchase and sale
addendum dated June 24th, 2002.  I'm going to ask you if you recognize your
signature on it.

A         Yes, I do.

MR. LAMER: Let's mark that as the next
exhibit.  That will be Exhibit 4.

EXHIBIT 4:  Contract
of purchase and sale addendum dated June 24, 2002

MR. LAMER:

Q         I'll
ask you to look at the initials here besides the words "made between
Dichicalow W. Korecki as seller and Aaron Pitt/Sherri Holt/William Holt as
buyer."  Do you see that?

A         Yes.

Q         Do
your initials appear before that?

A         Yes.

Q         You
didn't have your eyes closed when you did that; right?

A         No.

[…]

Q         You
saw that the purchasers were yourself, William Holt and Sherri Holt when you
signed that document?

A         I
didn't consider him a purchaser, but yes.

Q         You
saw that he was identified as a purchaser?

A         I
saw that he was on there.

Q         And
that didn't cause you any trouble?

A         No.

Q         No.
Because that was the deal, if I can put it that way?

A         Sure.

[
27
]

Further, Pitt only claims that he “assumed” that
William would hold the one-third interest in trust for the parties:

Q         Yes?

A         But
he needed to be on title, but there was no -- there was never any conversation
as to, you know, if the relationship was to end that he would acquire a
one-third interest because we were both contributing half to the mortgage
payments and we were both – the down payment came from mainly my side of the
family.

Q         Okay.
Continue.

A         So
I really trusted the fact that, you know, that I wasn't going to be swindled
out of what was rightfully mine.

Q         You
say "swindled."  Why do you say "swindled"?

A         Well,
I didn't think that he would claim one-third ownership as he held in trust for
me and Sherri.  He signed so that we could purchase the house, but I assumed
obviously that he didn't contribute to the investment, so there's no way that
he would assume one-third ownership.

Q         I
see.  You pronounced the word "in trust."  What does that mean to
you?

A         Well,
he held it.  Like, he signed it so that we could have the home.  And at a point
to where we wanted to move the property or sell it, then he wouldn't have a
right to it or he wouldn't have ownership of it.

Q         Did
you tell anyone about that?

A         When?

Q         About
the in-trust arrangement?

A         No.

Q         Did
it exist at the time that –

A         No.
There was no arrangement.  It was just what we both assumed, and there was no
reason for me to think otherwise.

Q         So
you assumed that he was holding in trust for whom?

A         For
Sherri and I.

Q         For
Sherri and yourself.  So you assumed that you were both 50 percent owner?

A         Yes.

Q         Or
did you assume that you were one-third owner and Sherri was one-third owner and
–

A         I
assumed that I was 50 percent owner of the home.

Q         Okay.
Notwithstanding you knew very well that the documents that you signed said
otherwise?

A         I
knew that he had to be on title for us to get the home, but I knew that I was a
50 percent owner of the home.

[
28
]

Thus, Pitt does not attest to the existence of
an agreement or arrangement to create a “trust”.  As defence counsel argues,
assumptions not communicated to the other side cannot be used to create a
contract.

[
29
]

Pitt’s counsel suggested at the hearing that
Pitt was entitled to argue the existence of a constructive trust, although
there is currently no pleading to this effect.  Defence counsel argues that,
even if the pleadings should be amended, such a plea would be bound to fail for
the very reason that, if an enrichment has occurred, then there is a “juristic
reason” for the enrichment, namely, the act of entering into a transaction
where sufficient consideration was exchanged in return for the transfer of
Pitt’s interest in the property.  Defence counsel asserts that unjust
enrichment as a cause of action does not entitle a court of equity to assess
whether the consideration exchanged under a valid contract is “fair” – this
jurisdiction exists under s. 65 of the
Act
and not under the
rules of equity.

[
30
]

At the time of the hearing, Pitt’s “in trust”
claim was based on an alleged actual trust agreement and not on the principle
of a constructive trust.

[
31
]

I find that on Pitt’s claim in the pleadings
that William holds title to a one-half interest in the property in trust for
and on behalf of the parties, that the defendants have met their onus to
negative, beyond a doubt, the existence of a bona fide triable issue.  On his
own admissions, no trust in Pitt’s favour can exist since he agreed to transfer
all his right, title and interest in the property to Holt pursuant to the terms
of the separation agreement.  Accordingly, the defendants are entitled to an
order pursuant to Rules 18(6) and 19(24) striking this plea.

VII.      The Misrepresentation Claim

[
32
]

Turning to the allegation of misrepresentation,
counsel contends that there is no merit to this claim.  Pitt testified that the
only misrepresentation made to him was Holt’s statement that William held
one-third of the property and that Pitt could not do anything about it.
However, Pitt admitted that he knew these misrepresentations to be false:

Q         Then
it goes on to say this: "She also made material misrepresentations to the
plaintiff in respect of the agreement, including material misrepresentations as
to the interest and entitlement of the defendant William Holt in the former
matrimonial home."  You said you agreed with that statement?

A         Right.

Q         So
what material misrepresentation are you talking about?

A         Well,
she said that he had a claim in the house and that I -- legally I couldn't --
that it had nothing I could do about it.

Q         Is
there anything else?

A         No.

[…]

Q         So
that discussion predated -- the misrepresentation about the agreement predated
the time that you first saw the agreement?

A         Yes.

Q         It
was to the effect that there was nothing you could legally do about her
father's one-third interest in the property?

A         Yes.

Q         And
in response to that, did you think of consulting a lawyer about it?

A         No.

Q         No,
so you just accepted that as the truth even though -- did you have confidence
in Ms. Holt?  Did you trust her?

A         I
didn't care at that point.

Q         Okay.

A         I
didn't necessarily trust her, but I didn't care.

Q         There
was a lot of animosity between the two of you that you described earlier today?

A         There
was some animosity.

Q         So
I put it to you that whatever it is that she said, you wouldn't have taken it
for granted one way or the other.

A         I
didn't care at that point.

Q         In
other words, you were prepared to do this deal whether or not those
representations were made to you?

A         Yes.

Q         Thank

47
]

Thus, contends counsel, Pitt now seeks to take
back the alleged benefit he put forward in the Provincial Court proceedings
through this action.  Counsel says that this is the very type of inconsistent
position that is at the centre of the doctrine of abuse of process.

[
48
]

Counsel also asserts that, in any event, Pitt
was unsuccessful on this point. Baird Ellan P.C.J. found, as follows:

[13]      The father helped with the mortgage
until August 2004 when the mother bought him out of the house for $27,900 [sic],
which reflected the return of his down payment less his share of an amount the
parties had borrowed from funds saved for one of the children.  Thereafter he
paid $300 under the separation agreement until January 2005, when the mother
returned to work full time after her stress leave.  The mother stayed in the
house and kept most of the furnishings.

[…]

[40]      Having regard to the considerations
provided for in the
Guidelines
and the
Act
as outlined above, as
I have said, it is in my view relevant that the mother pays for medical and
dental insurance, and receives a contribution toward rent and household
expenses from her new partner.  I have considered the father’s submission
regarding the amount he received back in respect of his contribution to the
purchase of the house.  Given the timing of the purchase, the amount of the
payments made over the months prior to separation, and the amount the father
would have spent on rent for that period, I am not in a position to find that
the amount he received should have been higher, nor that the agreement between the
parties relating to the house has relevance to the factors I must consider in
the applications before me.

[
49
]

Counsel says that it is this very finding that
Pitt is attempting to re-litigate and that as against Holt he is bound by issue
estoppel and cannot succeed.  Counsel asserts that this action is merely an
attempt to “re-hash” the same arguments that were rejected by Baird Ellan P.C.J.
As against William, counsel argues that the doctrine of abuse of process
described in
Toronto (City)
,
supra
, precludes Pitt from
re-litigating the issue.  Counsel contends that the full weight and cost of the
judicial system is being used against the defendants to extract money on the
basis of an argument which has already failed in the Provincial Court
proceedings.  Counsel says that this action is not only vexatious, but clearly
oppressive in the sense that legal expense required to try these issues is
bound to exceed what would be reasonable to spend in relation to the true value
of Pitt’s monetary claim.

[
50
]

The thrust of the defence argument on this point
is that the issue of the fairness of the separation agreement, having been
decided by Baird Ellan P.C.J., cannot be re-litigated in this action.  The
logic of the defence argument, as I understand it, is that having relied on the
separation agreement in the Provincial Court proceedings to attempt to reduce
his exposure to child maintenance payments, it is not now open for Pitt to
argue before this court that the separation agreement is unfair and should be
declared void.  The defence insists that Holt is entitled to rely on issue
estoppel and William on abuse of process to dismiss Pitt’s claim on the issue
of the fairness of the separation agreement.

[
51
]

While I find the defence submissions somewhat
compelling on this point, I cannot accede to the defence position.  In my
opinion, the cases relied upon by the defence to argue issue estoppel and abuse
of process do not apply in the instant case.  It is correct that Pitt relied on
the separation agreement as a ground for reducing his exposure to child
maintenance payments, but Baird Ellan P.C.J. simply rejected Pitt’s position on
this point.  In my view, she did not make any finding on the fairness of the
separation agreement, for the obvious reason that it was not an issue before
her.  The only issues before her were custody, maintenance and extraordinary
expenses.  She did note in her reasons that Pitt helped with the mortgage
payments until August 2004, when Holt bought him out of the property for
$27,900 [sic], which she states, “reflected the return of his down payment less
his share of an amount the parties had borrowed from funds saved for one of the
children.  Thereafter he paid $300 under the separation agreement until January
2005, when the mother returned to work full time after her stress leave.  The
mother stayed in the house and kept most of the furnishings.”  However, on the

s. 93(2)
argument put forward by Pitt, she did not make any finding on the
separation agreement – on the contrary, she states that she was not, “in a
position to find that the amount he received should have been higher, nor that
the agreement between the parties relating to the house has relevance to the
factors I must consider in the applications before me.”

[
52
]

In my opinion, the material does not establish
that Pitt is re-litigating factual claims made before the Provincial Court.  I
find that the defence argument that Pitt is barred in law from pleading that
the separation agreement is unfair and should be set aside must be rejected.

[
53
]

Finally, I reject the defence application for
security for costs.

[
54
]

The court has jurisdiction to order security for
costs be paid in the event that a triable issue is found to exist but the
proceeding itself has the hallmarks of an abuse of process: see
Novin v.
Novin
,
2004 BCCA 527
, 2004 CarswellBC 2250 (WLeC);
Gettliffe v.
Aguirre
,
[1996] B.C.J. No. 1317 (QL), 1996 CarswellBC 1384 (WLeC)
(S.C.)
.  The special circumstances relied upon in the instant case to support
the application of the authorities is the defence assertion that Pitt is
attempting to re-litigate claims that he has already lost, and that if he is
permitted to do so he should have to post security for costs given his
admission that he does not have the means to pay costs.

[
55
]

As found earlier in these reasons, I do not
agree with the defence contention that Pitt is re-litigating the fairness of
the separation agreement.  No doubt it appears that he is attempting to have it
both ways: rely on the separation agreement to reduce his exposure to a child
maintenance award in Provincial Court and when his position is rejected, bring
an action in this Court to set aside the separation agreement.  Nonetheless, it
cannot be said that the issue of the proper division of family assets has been
ruled upon, and I find that no grounds exist for an order of security for costs
against Pitt.

IX.       CONCLUSION

[
56
]

Holt and William are entitled to an order that:

(1)       The
“In trust” pleading is struck;

(2)       The
misrepresentation pleading is struck.

[
57
]

Hold and William are not entitled to an order
that the claim based on the fairness of the separation agreement should be
struck or dismissed as an abuse of process.

“B.I. Cohen J.”

The Honourable Mr. Justice B.I. Cohen
